utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I think we are hearing French translation. Is it only I or -- yes, everybody. I think it has been sorted out. Today we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Morrison being aware due to his official functions. Good morning, Mr. Markovic. Would you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of Rules of Evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering questions from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that provides evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal will ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind both of us to speak slowly and pause between our interventions so as to have everything recorded in the transcript. Mr. Markovic, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D7823 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the last page for the witness to see whether it is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement accurately reflect what you told my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you here in the courtroom today, would your answers be basically the same?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, I seek to tender the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna, any objections -- yes, I'll hear from you first, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. We're actually offering three documents as associated exhibits - that's 1D15062, 1D15098, and 1D15101 - and we would ask that they be added to our 65 ter list as we hadn't interviewed this witness at the time of our list being filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to -- excuse me -- to 1D15062. As regards 1D15098, the description -- the discussion of the document in paragraphs 11 and 16 of Mr. Markovic's statement are unclear, and it's unclear how the document supports the proposition in those statements, so we request that this be clarified live. And as regards 1D15101, the source and the date of this document are unclear, at least from the English translation, so we would request that this also be clarified live with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber shares the view of Ms. McKenna as regards 1D15098, and her comments is also fair enough as to the source and date of this document so they can be clarified with the witness by Mr. Karadzic directly. So we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement as well as 1D15062. Shall we give the number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The statement will be Exhibit D3073, and 1D15062 will be Exhibit D3074.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will read out summary of Mr. Obren Markovic's statement in the English language, and then we will go back to the document that needs some shedding light on. [In English] Mr. Obren Markovic was a member of the War Presidency of Brcko municipality and secretary of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence. He noticed that with the emergence of the multi-party system in BH, nationalist parties appeared and the SDA and the HDZ focused all of their political activities on the secession of BH. At pre-election rallies, the HDZ and SDA publicly declared unity by tying their party flags together. Obren Markovic considers that these activities were aimed at thwarting the Serbs' interests and these actions aroused fear and concern for their personal safety and that of their families. The armed conflict in Croatia also had a great impact on the overall political situation and security of all people in Brcko as many Serbs feared a repeat of the Second World War events. By mid-1991, some members of the National Guard Corps from Croatia appeared publicly wearing paramilitary uniforms, significantly worsening the security situation in the town and exacerbating the inter-ethnic tensions. At the same time, the Croats and the SDA organised check-points on the roads leading to Croatian and Muslim villages. Armed paramilitaries manned these check-points. As a result, the Serbs could not pass through on these roads and would be sent back. Mr. Obren Markovic later learned that the Muslims were also illegally arming themselves, receiving weapons from Sarajevo, and one from the Republic of Croatia. It was general knowledge that in 1991-1992 the Croatian leadership aimed to spread the armed conflict and war from the Republic of Croatia to BH as this would make their fight with the JNA easier. Obren Markovic is aware that the secretary of the Republican Secretariat of All People's Defence of BH issued an order to all municipal secretariats to obstruct the mobilisation of JNA units and to stop sending soldiers for military service, quickly followed by the SDA and HDZ leadership. This was to assist in the creation of conditions for secession as well as changes of personnel that were made, initiated from the top. This meant that mostly SDA and HDZ members were assigned to the key positions and the newly appointed national defence immediately began to violate the constitutions -- constitution and laws which were in force prohibiting the JNA mobilisation. The SDA and HDZ decided to impose further obstructions by blocking off the JNA units and commands in Brcko. When the Serbian people heard that the JNA could not carry out their basic tasks, they began organising themselves into guards in the parts of the town mostly populated by Serbs. In March and April 1992, the JNA, with a view of preserving peace in the territory of the municipality command in Brcko, tried to establish a unit that would be equally made up of the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. However, the Muslims and Croats widely rejected this initiative. Obren Markovic is aware that the Croatian military formations blew up the bridge across the River Sava on the eve of the Catholic Easter in 1992, and many who had visited Brcko for a holiday could not go back home. On the 1st of May, 1992, there was a further explosion which caused the bridge to collapse. This incident was falsely represented by the HDZ and SDA leaders. Because the Croatian military formations had damaged the bridge a month before, there were no vehicles on the bridge when the incident occurred. This incident was manipulated by the SDA and HDZ to place blame on the SDS and JNA. In some villages, the Muslims and Croats set up their paramilitary units as early as spring 1992. In villages that were surrounded by Muslim and Croat villages -- in the Serbian village that were surrounded by Muslim and Croat villages, mass crimes were perpetrated against the Serbs in all of them. Those Serbs who were not killed were either expelled or sent to camps. In three days, 63 Serbs were killed and all the others were expelled. In the afternoon of the 1st of May, 1992, an all-out attack was launched by the Muslims on Grcica, an area of the town populated by the Serbs only. This incident was well planned as all military facilities were targeted simultaneously and incidents began the war in Brcko. The Muslim-Croatian paramilitary formations in Brcko were so well organised and powerful that they managed to paralyse life and work in the municipality. The local authorities ceased to play any role whatsoever. Access to the hospital and the health centre were obstructed, so the Serbian people set up a makeshift medical station in Stanovi village where they provided medical care for the injured. On 3rd of May, 1992, a unit from the 22nd Light Partisan Brigade was mobilised to lift the blockade of the town, which was successful. A front line was established along the outer edge of the outlying suburbs. This remained same until the end of the war. The VRS had to defend this area, whereas the BH Army sought each day to penetrate the town. Throughout the war, the BH Army and HVO members aimed their artillery fire at the very centre of the town in an indiscriminate manner causing large-scale destruction of civilian facilities and killing or wounding a great number of civilians in the town. Cannons, tanks, howitzers and multiple-barrel rocket launchers were used to fire upon the town. Mr. Obren Markovic is aware that Serbs, Muslims and Croats lost their lives in equal numbers and women and children were also killed. Due to these attacks, civilians of all ethnicities tried to leave the territory. No one was expelled against their wishes. From the beginning of the armed conflict, the police station was split along ethnic lines, and the local authorities were in a state of general disarray. Criminals and paramilitaries -- paramilitary units took advantage of this period of anarchy and quickly gained control over the central urban zone. As the local authorities were unable to control the situation, the assistance of the republican organs and policemen arrived in the area and began to establish order. On 15th of May, many Serbs watched the death of JNA soldiers broadcast and television - that happened in Tuzla - which greatly aroused the fear around the Brcko inhabitants, in addition to the suffering of Serbs in the municipalities located upstream. Obren Markovic is aware that VRS 1st Posavina Motorised Brigade were informed about the positive humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions and did not commit crimes against BH Army soldiers who were taken prisoners. However, he is aware that members of the BH Army committed crimes against captured Serbian soldiers. [Interpretation] That was the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, since now you're going to deal with two associated exhibits, I'd like to deal with the one that we admitted already at the same time since it is referred to in the same paragraph, and given that it is an excerpt from a magazine article, it was not clear enough in what context it was referred to in that paragraph. Please continue. Yes, I meant 1D15062.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 1D10562 -- 1D15062. Can we enlarge it? The Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what magazine this is, Mr. Markovic? Can we go to the top of the page? There's probably a name there. I think it is the "Javnost."

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's called "Brcanski Pogledi."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it was a newspaper; right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know this Semso? Let me find his full name. What is the article -- well, let's see -- sorry. Can we see the left-hand side where it says by order of Jerko Doko, and can you explain to us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the time I was employed in the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence on mobilisation calls of the then JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When we received an order from our superior command, that is to say, the Tuzla Corps, to mobilise units of employees, workers' units, a small number of Croats and Muslims only responded to such call-ups. The then secretary of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence, Mr. Dzevdet Kehonjic told us that he had received from Jerko Doko, the republican secretary for national defence, a letter by which mobilisation and military exercises are being prohibited. However, pursuant to an order of our superior military commands, military training continued irrespectively, but by which time most of the Croats and Muslims no longer responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, does this suffice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D07848.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the second number. Apparently the two documents are related.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to tell us what it says on the certificate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 1D07848. By mistake it was not attached to the document that was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what this is, because we still do not have a translation.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a summons to serve in the armed forces. Such summons or call-ups were sent to all those who had war deployment before the war. Ivica Perikic, father's name Mate, is a Croat and he was summoned to respond to the assembly point 4128 on the 20th of September, 1991. Perhaps we can scroll down to see the note by our courier who returned from the field. The father of this person, Mato, refused to receive the summons and stated that he would throw a hand grenade at the barracks, which is something that actually repeated itself during demonstrations. And there is no record of anyone responding to the call-up, which was an obligation under the then Laws on Social Self-Protection and National Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3075, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D150 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 1D15101.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D15101.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are excerpts from the Muslim newspaper which was published during the war. I don't know what it's called, but this is what we got hold of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know this Semso Sakovic, and can you tell us what his position was and importance?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Semso Sakovic is engineer. Before the war he had worked in Brcko in a company, a construction company, I believe. When he received summons or draft papers, he showed up in the barracks once, but the next time around he did not. He was a member of the SDA leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is he discussing in this interview?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during briefings at the brigade command, we knew that the Muslim-Croat forces were being armed, and we were told such information every time. This document speaks to the fact that he himself confirmed our knowledge about the routes they received arms from Croatia and how weapons and equipment were being transported across the Sava River. And there's also mention here of the Brcko police which had documents to the effect that some boys were being discovered transporting weapons by policemen. Six rifles were found as well as 2.000 rounds and a machine-gun, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you said this was an interview. Why don't you put such questions to the witness? We know nothing about this document. I'm not sure if it is clear from the document itself. And Ms. McKenna's point was also related to the same point, what this document is about and when it was published.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems we cannot establish that, Your Excellency, but it's called "Dossier, Brcko residents prepare to resist aggression."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if we cannot establish such provenance, how can we admit it at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, how did you get a hold of this? It's a dossier rather than an interview, but he is being cited. How did you receive this article?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Right after the war, as Bosniaks, Muslims, and Croats were returning to Brcko town, communication began developing again, and thus we received their newspapers and they received ours. It was immediately after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did you receive this personally?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I received it from the vice-president of the Inmates Association of Republika Srpska, Mr. Nikola Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the 10th of June, 1991? Is that what we see in the first column? Is that when the war preparations started? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, I cannot ensure more than this, more information than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we do have a translation of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we do have the English translation, but still we are not sure about the provenance of the document. Have you formed your position, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll maintain our objection to the provenance of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you assist us, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think given that the witness has confirmed the contents are consistent with what happened in Brcko, that even though the -- even though the author of the document and when it was published is not known, that can be something that can go to weight, but since the witness has -- at least those parts that the witness has confirmed, it seems it should be admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this time the Chamber is not minded to admit this document since the provenance of the document is not clear. If the witness is able to confirm the content of the document, the accused still can put those questions to the witness. We'll not admit this. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, now I'm going to read this out to you, this position that is presented, and let's see what you know about that. It says: "In the area of the municipality of Brcko the first decision to start preparations for war" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's another way of putting a leading question. Why don't you put it in a more direct way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, is what is written here correct? Did you know at the time that Muslims in Brcko had started preparations for war the very moment when the SDA asked local committees to start preparing on the 10th of June, 1991?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: We were partly informed. We didn't know about all of this, but we did know about part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Irrespective of the text, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please bear in mind that if you start your question "Did you know," that that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you know about the preparations of Muslims for war in Brcko? When did they start, if they started at all, and how did they take place?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first information we received after the multi-party elections was that when they refused to respond to call-up into the only legitimate armed force at the time, that was the JNA, we started receiving information that through Sarajevo -- or, rather, through Croatia, special groups were being armed. Later on we found out that this was -- this was the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. From the then multi-ethnic SUP, MUP, information was coming in about weapons that were being found, weapons that were illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you mentioned children, taking advantage of children, of using children for transporting weapons. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you mean?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: From the police of Brcko district and the security organs, information was received that on the bridge between Croatia and Brcko weapons were found on children who were transporting weapons, and the bridge was damaged on the Croatian side at that point in time, and then the multi-ethnic police on the bridge found on these boys, as I've already said, six rifles, 2.000 bullets, and a machine-gun. This document that I proffered just shows what the police told us about before that. Mr. Semso Sakovic confirmed what this document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whose interest was to destroy the bridge the first time and the second time?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the destruction of the bridge from the Croatian side was aimed at preventing the JNA from getting into the Republic of Croatia because there used to be a garrison in Brcko. That was the aim of the Croatian side. As for the destruction of the bridge on this side, I really I don't know whose objective that was and who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that many victims that were being referred to, cars that were blown up on the bridge, et cetera. Can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, according to the information that we had at the brigade command, after the bridge was destroyed, this multi-ethnic commission from the SUP went out to the scene, a Muslim and a Serb, and from the military police there was a representative, too, and they identified the fact that there were corpses there, but I think that there was a very, very small number there. And the buses could not cross over because the bridge was already destroyed on the Croatian side. Or, rather, the MPs in the Brcko parliament discussed this topic after the war and an answer was never provided as the Bosniak or, rather, Muslim side always claims in terms of the number of casualties on the bridge. However, the reports say that there were people who were killed but a very small number, two or three, but nobody's established that for sure yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell us something else. You mentioned in your statement that that's when the war started, on the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd of May. Before that, were there any conflicts and incidents?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: After the bridge was destroyed, people were fleeing. The town was destroyed, and Croats were fleeing to Croatia, Serbs were fleeing towards Bijeljina, Serbia, and Muslims were fleeing in yet another direction so the city was practically abandoned. There was no fighting in town then. People had fled. On the morning of the 1st of May, at 2.00 in the afternoon, from the Muslim part of Dizdarusa facing the Serb part Grcica, the first mortar shell was fired. Of course the Serbs did respond from this other side, and then the attack was launched against the barracks where I was. Soon afterwards, the attack was repelled and there was no more fighting on that day in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell us whether the Serb side in Brcko had a paramilitary formation? I'm not talking about groups that came in after the war broke out, but at that point in time did you have any paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I have no questions at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you deal with 1D15098 as requested by Ms. McKenna. If you're not tendering it, we're fine with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we decided not to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Mr. Markovic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They're not interpreting this to me. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good. Mr. Markovic, I'd like to start with the issue that Mr. Karadzic finished with. Well, firstly, you'll confirm that you worked for the Municipal Secretariat for People's Defence in Brcko municipality from 1980, and then, as you said this morning, from 1991, you performed duties relating to recruitment and mobilisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, from 1980 as I was working at the Secretariat for National Defence, I worked on mobilisation issues and as I -- and also I worked as an inspector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The pace is too fast for interpretation. The witness will have to repeat the last two sentences. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you speak a bit more slowly for the benefit of interpreters and us all so that we can understand you better. The interpreters couldn't hear your last two sentences. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1980 I worked in the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence on mobilisation issues and also as an inspector, and in 1991, as I've already said, I worked on mobilisation issues in terms of the JNA or, rather, the armed forces of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to talk about the troops that were present in Brcko. You've just told the Court that there were no paramilitaries present prior to the conflict breaking out. And in paragraph 23 of your statement, you discuss the Muslim-Croatian paramilitary formations in Brcko that were so well organised and powerful that they managed to paralyse life and work in the Brcko municipality. I just -- and then you explain at paragraph 29 that once the armed conflict broke out, the local authorities were in a state of disarray, the police were totally disorganised, and the JNA left and so criminals and paramilitaries took advantage of this period and gained control -- quickly gained control of the central urban zone. So I'd first like to clarify the chronology on this. Mr. Markovic, Serb paramilitaries came to Brcko even prior to the war breaking out, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P2888.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. McKenna kindly speak into the other microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, the Court is familiar with this document. This is a summary of the events and situations in Brcko with an assessment of the degree of achievement, and it's by -- it's authored by the -- Djordje Ristanic of the Brcko Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm interested in page 3 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And I'm just going to put a passage from this to you. This document states that: "When the war started, various military formations started to arrive in Brcko to help out."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could skip down to -- if we could scroll down slightly. It states: "The first to arrive in Brcko was the group of instructors of Captain Dragan and that was about four to six months before the war. They formed a special unit including a large number of Brcko residents who went through training." And in the next paragraph it states: "The special unit was supposed to be under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Pavle Milinkovic, but it slowly became independent and evaded command." And it continues: "This contrasted with the early days, lasting about a month, when its activity was directed solely at the war and it made significant contribution. It had the support from a group of people from Brcko and this will be discussed later."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Markovic, this document shows that for the first month of the war, prior to the special unit getting out of hand, Captain Dragan's unit contributed to the war operations in Brcko. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall try to explain. I, or, rather, the military department of the National Defence Secretariat carried out full mobilisation into the Yugoslav People's Army. As for what is referred to here, we, or, rather, the then military department did not send a single military conscript into the units that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, is it your position that you did not know of a special unit which was originally under the command of the -- of the JNA commander Pavle Milinkovic of 70 people? Is it your position that you did not know of the existence of this unit?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that these units existed, but at the time we did not send military conscripts, soldiers, to these units. We heard of the existence of these units, but we as the military department did not send any conscripts there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So just to clarify your testimony on this, you were, in fact, aware of paramilitary units present in Brcko prior to the conflict breaking out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, that is not correct. I've been trying to explain. Not a single paramilitary unit was in Brcko legally, because we did not send people to these units. That's why I say that we don't know about that, that I don't know about that. We heard of their existence, but we did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, yesterday Mr. Pero Markovic, a War Presidency member, testified - this is at T 34734 - that the War Presidency asked for assistance from Bijeljina and that Serb troops came to Brcko in response to that request. Now, do you agree that when the conflict broke out, a large number of troops came to Brcko from Bijeljina to assist the Brcko authorities?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 3rd of May, 1992, one unit, the so-called 22nd Light Partisan Brigade, was manned, because it had existed already in terms of establishment, but some people from Bijeljina whose wartime assignment was Brcko, even beforehand, came there. These persons, these soldiers, came half dressed in military terms. They had very few weapons, and they were lined up at the barracks where I was, and I saw this column of men. This was on the 3rd of May, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's talk about who the men from Bijeljina were. These men that came included both paramilitaries and police, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: These people that I'm speaking of are not the people that you're speaking of. These are people who were deployed to the so-called 22nd Light Partisan Brigade, and they were deployed for the defence of the town of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, yesterday Mr. Markovic confirmed at T 34735 that paramilitaries, including -- that Serbian guards under the command of Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer, and a unit of radicals under the command of Mirko Blagojevic were present in Brcko. Is it your position that you do not know -- did not know that these paramilitaries were present in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I knew they were in Brcko, those units, Mauzer. I did know them personally but I knew that they were there. However, we had nothing to do with these forces. We were manning the 22nd -- or, rather, the 395th Motorised Brigade or, rather, the 1st Posavina Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The paramilitaries, Mr. Markovic, came to Brcko at the request and with the support of the Serb authorities, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we see P2889, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now if we look at the first long paragraph in this -- sorry, this is an Eastern Bosnia Corps command intelligence report to the VRS Main Staff from the chief of intelligence -- or sorry, to the chief of intelligence and security administration dated 29th of September, 1992, and it's discussing the events in Brcko. And in the middle of the first large paragraph it states -- and it's discussing the groups that came to Brcko, it states: "We also believe that there were groups who came as ordered, i.e., who had the support of the then military and civilian authorities. Here we mean the leadership in Bijeljina, which in fact had brought 550 gathered fighters at the very beginning the war. The most notorious of all were Mauzer and Major Gavrilovic with Arkan's escort led by Peja and the civilian authorities in Bijeljina." So, Mr. Markovic, this document shows that paramilitaries, including Mauzer and Gavrilovic, came to Brcko with the support of the Bijeljina authorities, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm unaware of any of that. I wish to explain this. Mauzer and Blagojevic, they were in Brcko, but who asked them to come, who gave them orders or directives, that is something I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Mirko Blagojevic and his troops?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And that's P901, please. I'm sorry, I must -- my apologies. It's P2901.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This, Mr. Markovic, is an interview with Mirko Blagojevic on the Serbian TV programme "My Guest, My Truth."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we can have page 9 of the English and page 12 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript should reflect that it is his truth, the guest's truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could focus on the large paragraph of text, statement by Mr. Blagojevic. And he's -- he's discussing the importance of winning the battle for Brcko and he states halfway down through that text: "Fortunately, we arrived at that war theatre at the right moment, put ourselves at the disposal of the then Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Brcko, of Serbian Brcko, of Mr. Bosko Maricic, and said that we were at their disposal and to tell us what needed to be done and where." And he continues in his next response -- or he continues at the end: "We had good co-operation with the officers who were at the barracks in Brcko at that time." He goes on: "I must praise Mr. Manojlovic, who I believe was the barracks' commander then, and must praise Mr. Peja Milinkovic, Captain Sehovac, for receiving us well. We co-operated well. We took control of the city very quickly." So, Mr. Markovic, in fact, rather than filling the void after the JNA left as you suggest at paragraph 29 of your statement, the paramilitaries worked together with the Brcko Crisis Staff and the JNA to take control of the city, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the police then. At paragraph 29, you state: "The police station split along ethnic lines, and as far as I know, there were around eight Serbian policemen who remained in town and were totally disorganised." In fact, Mr. Markovic, there were many policemen present in Brcko from the start of the war, including many police troops from Bijeljina, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When I stated that, that was the 1st of May, that is to say, when the bridges were destroyed. That's when the police station -- well, the Muslims went to the Muslim part of town and the Croats went to the Croatian part of town of the municipality of Brcko, that is, and only a very small number of Serbs who were policemen stayed on. What you are referring to, I assume, pertains to the reserve police force that was later mobilised in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard evidence, Mr. Markovic, that the Serbian public security station was established on the 2nd or 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And that, for the parties' reference, is Djordje Ristanic's statement, P3023 at paragraph 164. And if I can call up P2763, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This, Mr. Markovic, is a letter from the president of the Bijeljina Security Services Centre to the minister of the interior dated 7th of May, 1992. And it states in the third paragraph down: "Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Semberija and Majevica SAO, TO units and some troops from the active and reserve police from Bijeljina, Ugljevik and Lopare were sent to Brcko exclusively in order to protect public and private property by securing buildings and trying to normalise life in the war outside -- the area outside the war operations. According to reports from Brcko, the police are carrying out that role." And it continues: "About 150 policemen have been there since the beginning. According to recent reports, the public security station is now operational." So, in fact, Mr. Markovic, from the very beginning of the war there were multiple policemen present in Brcko, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. After the destruction of the bridges on the 1st of May, 1992, the police station in Brcko was practically disbanded. It fell apart. There were to policemen, save the ones I mentioned, save for the ones I mentioned. On the 7th of May and later on, there began a mobilisation wave of the reserve police force in order to establish law and order, because by that time paramilitary formations had already started looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, Brcko police SJB employee Petar Kaurinovic confirmed to this Trial Chamber that on his arrival at Brcko SJB on the 3rd of May, 1992, there were lots of police officers there, and that's at T 34124. So again, I put it to you that there were many police officers present in Brcko Public Security Station from the outbreak of the conflict, from at least the 3rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the service of the then military department where I worked, which was in charge of mobilisation of military conscripts into the reserve force of the police station and the armed forces units as well as the civilian protection, was not engaged in this. Now, who said that they came upon a large number of policemen is something I don't know, but there are documents in existence as to when we carried out the mobilisation of the police reserve force for the police station in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Markovic, in your statement you said that the police station was totally disorganised. So let's look at how effectively they functioned at the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P3003. Now, these are minutes of the meeting of the specialist board of the Serb SJB held on 2nd June 1992, and if we can go to the last page briefly, the last page of both the -- the English and B/C/S. Sorry, that would be the -- thank you. You'll see that they -- these minutes were agreed on the 2nd of June, 1992, by Brcko SJB head Dragan Veselic. Now, I'd like to go back to the first page of the document, please. I'm sorry, page 3 of the English and page B/C/S -- or page 7 of the B/C/S. And if we focus on the section heading "Crime."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So this is the Brcko SJB discussion of events in the public security station, and it says: "The affairs and tasks in the field of crime have been functioning from the very division, i.e., the establishing of the Brcko SJB. "Considering that the function of the head is being filled by a man who is directly engaged in affairs from the jurisdiction of the state security, it was agreed that his deputy be named as soon as possible. It was also agreed that all detention measures, rulings on the detention of certain people be recommended and submitted in writing to the Brcko SJB head by the head of crime department." So, Mr. Markovic, on the 2nd of June, 1992, rather than describing a situation where the police are not functioning, this document states that affairs and tasks in the field of crime have been functioning from when the Brcko SJB was taken over at the start of the war. Now, this is a more accurate reflection of the situation in Brcko at that time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this information comes from the police station, and it is dated the 2nd of June, 1992. On the 7th of May, 1992, as it says here, the mobilisation of the reserve force began in order to establish the police station which had literally not existed before. This part probably, although I don't know because it's a police report, I don't know how it functioned, but I do know that paramilitary formations in Brcko were robbing people, breaking into apartments, stealing vehicles, et cetera. As for what is contained in the report, it is a police station report and I'd rather not comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the paramilitaries then. At paragraph 29 you describe the criminals and paramilitary formations who took advantage of this period of anarchy and quickly gained control of the central urban zone. Now, this central urban zone included the Luka camp, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As for Luka, I heard about it in the barracks, and I was never in the Luka camp. It is some 300 metres away from the barracks only.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, there's evidence before the Trial Chamber that from the 4th of May, 1992, through July 1992, non-Serbs were detained in Luka camp during which period they were beaten, abused, including sexual abuse and rape, and many were killed. So let's discuss -- or do you agree that these events occurred in Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: We heard about it and only heard about it because that was the story that went around town. Everyone talked about it, talked about the existence of the Luka camp, but officially we weren't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about one of the people -- one of the people who were committing crimes at Luka camp, that's Ranko Cesic. Were you aware that Ranko Cesic had committed crimes in Brcko generally, including at Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it. I heard that Branko Cesic committed certain crimes in the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cesic was first indicted by the ICTY on the 21st of July, 1995, for crimes committed in Brcko, including at Luka camp and -- including at Luka camp in May and June 1992. Were you aware that this indictment had been issued?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I learned of it later on. I didn't know about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cesic was arrested in Belgrade by the FRY authorities on the 25th of May, 2002, and transferred to The Hague on the 17th of June, 2002. Were you aware that he had been arrested and transferred to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cesic was a member of the Brcko SJB during the period he committed crimes for which he was indicted, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Mr. Cesic was a member of both the police and army. However, he was a member of the police, although some policemen and some members of the military infiltrated into the paramilitary formations which committed crimes around Brcko. It is true, although I don't know when exactly, that Cesic was a member of the police at first, and later on, due to the criminal activities, he was fired from the police. I assigned him -- or we, the military department, assigned him to the army. Even today I'm in charge of the military records, and I have that information, although I don't know it by heart.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter number 23191.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: This is a certificate dated the 5th of July, 2002, from the Brcko department of the Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence signed by you as the head of the department. And in the final paragraph -- or I'm sorry, the certificate certifies that Ranko Cesic was a member of the Army of the Republika Srpska, that is, a member of the armed forces of the former SFRY, during the period from 15th May 1992 until 26 June 1992, as a member of SJB Brcko. And it shows that he continued to serve in the VRS in military post Brcko from July to October 1992. So in this document you certified that Cesic was a member of the Brcko SJB during the period in which he was committing crimes at Luka camp, and you did so just a few weeks after Mr. Cesic had been transferred to the ICTY to answer for those crimes. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the date, but this document before us, even today if a member of Ranko Cesic's family came to ask for it would receive it, if authorised. This is an official record of war participation that is kept for every conscript. There's nothing in dispute. As for your suggestion that it was issued before his arrival here, that's something that I'm unaware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, after leaving the Ministry of Defence, you went to work for the service of -- for the protection of war veterans and invalids; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Can you explain where you -- where you worked after 2007?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In 2007, when Brcko district was established, all military records that I worked on in Brcko as well as all of the staff, the six of us, were moved to Pelagicevo, the neighbouring municipality, alongside all of the military records. In 2007, the ministries of -- the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska is shut down and the unified Ministry of Defence for Bosnia-Herzegovina was established. In 2008, I returned together with all of the military files to Brcko. Nowadays I work for the service of -- for benefits for veterans and war invalids with three constituent parts, Bosniak, Croat, and Serb. I'm in charge of the Serb component, and that is my job today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 24658. I'm afraid -- I don't think that we have received a translation for this document yet. But you'll see this document is a letter dated 11th September 2009, from the Service for the Protection of War Veterans and Individuals, Military Records Unit. If we could go to the second page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you'll agree, Mr. Markovic, that it's signed under your -- on your authority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And if we could return to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You'll see -- can you identify the individual at the first entry? Just his name.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is about Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And could we scroll down, please, to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And if you could identify the two individuals at the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Branko Pudic and Konstantin Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So in this document, Mr. Markovic, you are confirming that these individuals were members of the police for the relevant dates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, these and other police officers from the -- from Brcko were placed by Witness Izet Gasi at Luka camp, and that's at T 16612 to 16615. So, Mr. Markovic, I put it to you that in fact rather than the organs of local authorities ceasing to play any role whatsoever as you stated at paragraph 29 of your statement, the police were actively involved in the crimes at Luka camp. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the claim that the police committed crimes at the Luka camp is not correct. Maybe some members of the police, as Ranko Cesic, but not the police generally as you said. I don't think that the police committed crimes at the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different topic. At paragraph 33 of your statement you say that both Muslims and Croats lived in the Brcko area for the duration of the war. Now you'll agree, Mr. Markovic, that Brcko went from a town where the Serbs were a minority to a town where Serbs were a majority. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And it -- I'm sorry. And I'm going to read a statement from Mr. Karadzic to you at the National Assembly session of the 11th of May, 1994, where he states: "We have never been a majority in Brcko, but we were always the third, but we have to solve that with a combination. We cannot call upon one principle that is ethnic and historical. We have to call upon the principle of new 'fakticitet.' That is the vital interest for the Serbian people and there is no discussion. This is not important town for the Muslims, but it is important to us."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: For the party's reference, that's at page 40 of the English and page 35 of the B/C/S of P1390.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Markovic, Mr. Karadzic's statements -- statement reflects the reality of what happened in Brcko in that it was a town of great strategic interest to the Serbs which Serbs were determined to gain and retain control over. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean the Brcko municipality, the one from before the war, the Muslims are even now the majority population in Brcko, and they used to be the majority. If we are talking just about the town of Brcko, there were many people who moved in who were refugees from other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They have become the inhabitants of Brcko as they cannot go back to their own homes, but -- and the majority of Croats and Muslims have moved back into their old homes in Brcko. In spite of that, in the Brcko municipality as a whole, there are more Muslims than Serbs even now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P1490. And I'm interested in pages -- page 44 of the English and page 42 of the B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this is a meeting -- or this is an excerpt from Ratko Mladic's notebooks, and it details a meeting on the 20th of March, 1996, with a delegation from Brcko Municipal Assembly, and you are listed as present at this meeting, and I'd like to focus on what president -- the municipality president, Pajic, states. He tells Mladic: "We wanted to visit you to give you support, to thank you and acquaint you with what we're doing. Brcko has 32.500 inhabitants now and about 26.000 inhabitants have arrived. We need to settle about 7.000 inhabitants if the town is to be protected." And then towards the bottom of the page he states: "There has been an influx of Muslims in Brcko." Now, by the town being protected, Mr. Pajic meant ensuring that Brcko remained Serbian, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Pajic meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to play a video. That is 65 ter number 40606A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Regarding us who live in Brcko and Posavina, I think the situation is the same over here. If you remember, Brcko was divided up to the railroad, up to Brka, this way, that way. We are sure that Brcko will not and must not be divided, that Brcko will remain Serbian, and that it will serve as a connection between Krajinas and motherland Serbia. And that in future in the Serbian lands, Interplet socks, Bimal oil, Bimeks ham, et cetera, will continue to be sold. That is to say that we will serve as the connection between all Serbian lands in proportion to their future size. And I sincerely hope that they will become as big as we all want them to be."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Markovic, they were the views of Pero Markovic, a member of the Brcko municipality authorities, on this issue. Do you accept that, as both Mr. Markovic and Mr. Karadzic stated, Brcko was of key strategic interest to the Serbs and Serbs were determined that it remain Serbian?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: These are political statements, and the interest of the Serbian people in Brcko was to connect the Krajina in Serbia because of the corridor, because of medications, the problems with treating people in the western part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The witness hasn't confirmed anything about the video. I'm wondering why it wasn't tendered with the other witness who could have spoken more directly to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the Prosecution didn't receive the video until during the witness's testimony yesterday, and it was disclosed to the Defence shortly thereafter. Mr. Zec didn't have an opportunity to review it until after the witness's testimony. But as to the connection with this witness, Mr. Markovic was present at a video where -- excuse me, was present at an interview where the interest in protecting the Serbian nature of Brcko was discussed, and he stated that he didn't know what that was meant by it. So this goes to impeachment. And in fact, his -- just if I may add, Mr. Markovic's -- what Mr. Markovic has stated about the video does confirm the content, in that he stated that it was in the interest of people -- Serbian people in Brcko to connect the Krajina in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will not accept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for the witness. I would just seek to tender 65 ter number 24658, which is -- was the letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: -- which I omitted to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we have the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Sorry. If we could tender it MFI, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there would be no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that we had translations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your information is obviously more up-to-date than mine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From the Registry. Yes, we will accept it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we have your re-examination after the recess? We will take a break for half an hour and resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have several questions, Mr. Markovic, just to clarify something so that we will dispel a confusion. When I asked you about Serbian paramilitary formations and also Muslim and Croatian paramilitary formations, I asked you whether before the war you had prepared the paramilitary formation composed of the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, no, we didn't have it. I have already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the Muslims and the Croats have paramilitary formations composed of the local people?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They had barricades. They had armed paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 21, you were asked about the instructors and their students who were under Milinkovic's command for a while, and then later on they became independent. While they were under Milinkovic's command, could they be considered a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: All those who were under the command of the 1st Posavina Infantry Brigade and under the command of Pavle Milinkovic could not have been in paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could your service conduct investigations if it learned that someone had a doubtful past or had a criminal record? Were you allowed to conduct investigation?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed to conduct investigations. We had a different role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you do about people who you learned were in the position of authorised officials but they also had criminal records?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: If they were not convicted but they were conscripts, they were assigned to military units, and they were, as is normal, under the control of the unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that something new that you received as instructions from us or what sort of procedure was it? When did it date from?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It dated from the beginning the war when we received instructions from you, that is to say, from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I know that you were not in the police, but during the cross-examination you were asked whether you were aware of the possible number of those who were stripped by the police of their status of authorised officials and who were made to be ordinary soldiers.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the numbers, but whoever violated the rules of the police were dismissed from the police. We received reports. We called such people, and we assigned them to the Army of Republika Srpska until the time when they had to go and serve their sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about Ranko Cesic and some records were shown to you. It was said that you confirmed that it was so. Is it you who confirmed or is it evidence that cannot be changed?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It's evidence that cannot be changed. It's confirmation from the MUP. In the procedure of registering documents, we would receive feedback for each person, that is to say, either from the police or from the MUP, about the dates during which this person was on police or military duty, and this would be included in the personnel files. And according to the laws of Republika Srpska, this is to be kept for 70 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Cesic himself, do you know what was the attitude of the police chief to him; that is to say, was Cesic staying in Luka and acting in Luka on the orders or with the approval of the police chief?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the police chief, Dragan Veselic -- or, rather, the chief of the CSB, did not know that Cesic was doing what he was doing and especially not that he issued him orders to commit any sort of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the majority. In the town, were there settlements where one of the three ethnicities was the majority?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were settlements in Brcko where one ethnicity was the majority. For example, Klanac was with the majority Muslim population and Stari Varos with the majority Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Srpska Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From when does that name date, Srpska Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat his answer because the exchange is way too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please take a look at the transcript, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the last answer, because it has not been recorded. You said that you were born 60 years ago.

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it dates from more than 100 years back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And in the parts that remained under Serbian control, were there also Muslims and Croats living there as a relative minority, and did they continue to live there during the war?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the authorities, the authorised officials, towards these people?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to explain. After the bridges were blown up - we talked about the destruction of the bridges - all of those who remained in Brcko, whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims, and there were many of them, were involved in one of the Defence structures and they had all the rights and obligations in accordance with the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army. Likewise after the war, when the war finished, many people, and I'm familiar with the records, many Muslims and Croats exercised their rights according to the law on the rights of fighters and veterans of Republika Srpska. They entered their apartments, they received money and so on. So there was no difference at all between the ethnicities, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims, if they participated in the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you now please tell us what was the difference between the Muslims who stayed with you and the Muslims who did not stay with you, who left, and who shot around in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: OBREN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Those who stayed on live there to this day, and those who left again came back and they tried to continue living in Brcko as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Markovic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Markovic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour -- excuse me. While --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: While the next witness is brought in, may I just make a brief request to amend P6147, which is an exhibit tendered through Petar Kaurinovic. The exhibit is excerpted pages from Mr. Kaurinovic's previous OTP interview which includes quotes that the witness didn't confirm when he testified before you. And I noticed yesterday that -- well, at T 34139, I quoted from -- to Mr. Kaurinovic from page 62 of his OTP interview and tendered that page. However, yesterday I noted that the quote started on page 62 but went on to page 63, so I should have actually also tendered that. So I request that that page 63 of his interview be added, subject, of course, to any comments Mr. Robinson has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. I take it you have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done. Thank you, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A good opportunity, perhaps, for me, Mr. President, to note that with respect to what we foreshadowed yesterday, the addition of one or two pages to P6164, in fact I discussed that with Mr. Robinson and there was just one additional page that was omitted and that would be page 61 of the English and page 60 of the B/C/S, which is just one page immediately before the -- one of the series began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, that will be done. You confirm that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bojanovic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please let us pause between questions and answers and also let us speak slowly so that it can all be reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you see the transcript before you, once my question is typed out and when you see the letter A, which is supposed to signify "answer," then it would be a good thing if you started answering only then. Do you see the transcript?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7824. Could we please see that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the statement that you gave to the Defence team on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was quite fast. Please do pause.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read this statement? Have you signed it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this statement faithfully reflect everything you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom, would your answers basically be the same as the ones you gave in this statement?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Basically they would be the same. Perhaps something could be added, but the essence is the same as what is written up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I'd like to tender this package.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Bojanovic, you were kind enough to bring us some court documents. I don't have the translations yet, so I will have to ask you viva voce about those documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the meantime, I would like to tender the package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us about the associated exhibits Mr. Karadzic is also tendering, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're tendering three associated exhibits. The first is 1D07240, and we would ask that that be added to our 65 ter list as we didn't have it at the time that list was filed. The second is 1D25456, and the third is 1D08664.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards the two exhibits, 1D07240 and 1D25456, the Chamber finds it a bit difficult to figure out how they are relevant and what in context they are referred to in each paragraph. So I would like the accused to deal with those two judgements as well. Otherwise, any objection, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. And I seek leave to remain seated again still. Your Honour, 1D25456 is 33 pages in length, and five of those pages have been translated but not the actual document that is cited in support of the sentence in the statement so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that was one of the reasons I asked Mr. Karadzic to lead live to see the relevance. So we'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're done, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Then we'll admit the 92 ter statement as well as 1D8664.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D3076 and D3077 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out in the English language the summary of Judge Savo Bojanovic's testimony. [In English] Savo Bojanovic was a judge of the Military Court in Bijeljina. When the inter-ethnic tensions escalated in mid-1991, along with the aspirations of the leadership of Croatia and Slovenia and eventually BH to secede from Yugoslavia, Savo Bojanovic was mobilised into the JNA. He was engaged for about 15 days before being discharged and returning home. In around June-July 1992, after the formation of the Army of Republika Srpska, VRS, it was shown to be necessary to establish Military Courts. An appeal was made for professionally trained judges to sit in these courts, and a number of people responded, including Savo Bojanovic. The candidates were interviewed and tested. They were selected solely on the basis of moral and professional qualifications. They were not selected on the basis of connections or political affiliation, and to his knowledge, none of the judges in the court were a member of the SDS or any other party. Savo Bojanovic later discovered that mandatory security checks conducted by VRS security organs were carried out on the candidates, ensuring no political interference in the selection of the judges. The Military Courts were then established in mid-July 1992. The work of the Military Courts was independent and no interference from the outside was allowed by anyone, including military and civilian authorities. The work of the court and all of the judges was based solely on compliance with the enforcement -- with an enforcement of the law taken from the former SFRY. All suspected perpetrators of criminal offences enjoyed equal treatment by the court regardless of their religion or ethnic background.
