utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojanovic. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, but only clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you do so. Are you not tendering any of the documents you showed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I omitted to do that. Yes, I seek to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with one by one. Are you also tendering 1D7421, dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't mind it being admitted at all, but I just want to point out that there's a translation now and this was an associated exhibit, and Ms. Sutherland sent me an e-mail saying that they object to it being used as an associated exhibit because it wasn't translated. And they have a translation and now they want to offer it as a Prosecution exhibit. So we don't mind it being admitted, but we think it ought to be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The translation was done this morning while we were sitting in court, so at the time that I made my objection we had to translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it matters in which form we should admit the evidence. We'll admit it as Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next, 2471 -- 713 and 24714. You do not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit them all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P6182 and P6183 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bojanovic, can you please help us to understand whether prisoners of war who did not commit any crime were someone to be tried by the military courts?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why are they then held in detention?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is the purpose for them to be punished or to be tried or to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose this had to do with exchange. This was what people said, if you mean specifically Batkovic, that the inmates of the camp were used to be exchanged for Serbian soldiers who had been taken prisoners at other fronts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the Red Cross visit this prison? I mean the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I omitted to say, though it's included in my written statement, that after the double murder within the Vanekov Mlin compound, on the following morning a delegation the International Red Cross which controlled Batkovic heard about the incident and that a double murder had occurred. The delegation consisting of five men and myself as the investigating judge who was doing the on-site investigation and the presiding judge of the Military Court, perhaps the deputy prosecutor also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters haven't heard the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- came along and asked me to show them everything that I had done, even though this was not in our jurisdiction, but there was no reason for me not to show it them. So I showed them the on-site investigation report and the photo file and also the issue -- the order to issue the wanted notice which I had forwarded to the MUP on that morning. So we handed over all the documents for inspection to the representatives of the ICRC, and I think there was a Swiss lady in the delegation who was heading this team.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I'm very late in my objection, but how does the Red Cross visiting Batkovic camp arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked whether that's a detention facility or a camp, so I think he can touch upon this issue. Please continue in any event, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, as a military judge and as a lawyer, can you just remind us of the names of perpetrators? What was the case in which the ICRC came to visit you the follow morning which you just described to us?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This was the murder of two Muslims on the premises of Vanekov Mlin. The head of one was cut off and the other person was killed from a firearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the names, really, but we have the on-site investigation report. That's available and it contains the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a lawyer, can you tell us if there are situations in which both -- in which the civilians are also treated as prisoners of war? Is there some kind of activity that civilians may engage in which represents a basis for them to be taken prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. If they were supporting an armed force or associates of it, then there is a basis for them to be treated as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let me not pursue this any further. On page 82 you were asked about being investigating judge and therefore being able to arrest someone and so on and so forth. I have to tell you that the differences in court systems are great so can you tell the Trial Chamber to whom does an investigating judge issue orders and who is then trying to arrest someone on behalf of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The police. A court does not make the arrest. The police does that. The only thing that the court does is makes the decision requesting somebody's detention. A judge does not have the authority to arrest anyone. He can just issue the order on detention if the conditions as set by law have been met and if the reasons which are all enumerated in the law also exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 77 and 78, you were asked about the murder of a Serb by a sniper and the two and a half years' sentence. The Prosecution suggests that our military courts would sentence harshly those who murdered Serbs as opposed to those who murdered the Muslims who were not sentenced so harshly. In this case, both the killer and the killed were Serbs. Why was this perpetrator sentenced to only two and a half years' sentence?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This was manslaughter and this is why this person was only sentenced to two and a half years. It was manslaughter. However, if I may add, once the -- we decided on the sentence, we did not -- we were not guided by the ethnicity of the perpetrator or the victim. If there were aggravating circumstances, then the sentence was adequate, it was appropriate, regardless of the fact whether it was a Serb or a Muslim or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: P6182 is the case that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the murder of Djuric in which I was responsible for the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see D1756, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the jurisdiction, the subject matter jurisdiction, I'm not sure whether about the territorial jurisdiction as well, but the subject matter and the distinction between the military and civilian judiciary. So I would ask you to look at this document together with me. You made a correction and said that this was in 1993. This was in paragraph 16. Please have a look at this Official Gazette dated the 31st of December, 1993, and tell us whether these are the Laws on the Military Judiciary and the Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that it's the Law on the Military Prosecutor's Office. Yes, the date is the 31st of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the change in the laws which took place in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, even though at the time I was already out of the Military Court. But I know that the consequence of the attitude about the subject matter jurisdiction between the regular and Military Court was the adoption of the Law on the Military Prosecutor's Office where it was specified in which cases the military prosecutor's office was to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at page 4 now, and in English we can keep the page that we can see now, but we need page 4 in Serbian, and the title, how it begins, and then we shall move on to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this my decree on the proclamation of the Law on Military Courts on the 30th of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at Article 10. Both in Serbian and in English, we shall need the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what Article 10, paragraph 2, says?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The military courts shall try military personnel and other persons for the following crimes and then the crimes are listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it say here? What crimes are these?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in Article 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are mostly military crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, please, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean after the numbers. Military courts --

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "Shall try military and other personnel for criminal acts committed against military installations, criminal acts committed while on duty or concerning the performance of duty, as well as those committed in the army if the targets are combat equipment, weapons, ammunition or explosives which serve the country's defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I'm here listening to court reporter who cannot possibly keep up. She's been polite enough not to scream but I think she'd like to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mm-hmm. Yes, your reading was far too fast. Yes, what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was whether this is the law or, rather, the amendment that you mentioned during the cross-examination and which was introduced in 1993.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the consequence of an attitude taken in view of the distinction of subject matter jurisdiction between civilian and military courts. The consequence was the adoption of the Law on Military Courts and Military Prosecutor's Office which occurred, as we can see from this document, in late 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now you spoke a bit slower. What does that mean that an attitude is taken and then a law is amended? How much time is necessary to adopt a law after a change of position?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably two or three months pass between the two. I left the Military Court in late September 1993 and the position had already been defined. It was known exactly in which case the Military Court was to do something and in which case it was the civilian court. The position was that all the cases in which the proceedings had begun should be completed by the Military Court, and it so happened that the law that regulated and legalised all this was adopted in late 1993, towards the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked today on pages 75 -- actually, 75 to 76, about release from pre-trial custody. Could you please tell us what all the reasons are for that? Can there be a procedural reason for that? Does the Prosecution have to meet certain dead-lines?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, the first reason why persons are released from custody is if the period involved had expired. The investigating judge could send a person into custody for 30 days and then the chamber could extend it for another 30 days.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or 60 days, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the Supreme Military Court could decide on an extension of another 90 days. Now what are the reasons except for the expiry of dead-lines. They are in the Law on Criminal Procedure. Custody can be ordered in order to prevent influencing witnesses. If all the witnesses had been heard in the pre-trial stage, then there is no reason to continue custody. If there is a threat of flight, also if a passport is taken from the accused, then that reason is no longer there, so there's no need for me to go into all the reasons that are listed in the Law on Criminal Procedure. It is up to the investigating judge to see whether the reasons are still there, and if the military prosecutor's office does not oppose this release from custody, then such a release is legal and legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if the term involved expires and if there is no further request for extension, what happens?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If there are no further reasons for the custody to continue, then the judge decides to end custody as I did in the case that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we did not catch the names of all the cases that were listed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my question, although I spoke slowly, there is something missing. I asked what happens if there is no indictment, and if there is no request for extension and custody is over? Actually, it's the part concerning indictment that was missing. 2464 is the 65 ter number I'd like to see now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 65 ter. 664.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Law on Criminal Proceedings. 24664.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was admitted earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As Exhibit 6178.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Page 3, please, in Serbian. In English we can keep this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Bojanovic, could you present Article 190 to us. What does it prescribe?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 1, Article 190, custody may be ordered only under the conditions envisaged in this law. That means that custody may be ordered only under the conditions envisaged in this law. And then number 2 says the duration of custody, the duration of custody must be kept to the shortest necessary time. It is the duty of all bodies and agencies participating in criminal proceedings and of agencies extending them legal aid to proceed with particular urgency if the accused is in custody. That means that custody means depriving a person of its freedom. It is proceedings that have to establish whether somebody had indeed committed a crime. That is why custody is a sensitive matter invariably. And that is why the legislator says that in such cases one should act with urgency so that people are not detained without any reason. Number 3, throughout proceedings custody shall be terminated as soon as the grounds on which it was ordered cease to exist. This is precisely what I spoke of a moment ago as I responded to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 4 in English, Article 197, and we can find it in Serbian too. In Serbian it's page 5 and in English it's page 4. 197, paragraph 3, that means that we need the next page in English. Could we please zoom in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, can you read paragraph 3 only.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3. If the -- if the indictment is not brought before the expiration of the periods referred to in paragraph 2 of this Article, the accused shall be released. That is precisely what we discussed already. Mihajlovic Rade, the indictment had not been issued and all the time periods had expired, 30 days, 60 days, so it was proper and lawful to abolish the decision on custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1476. Could we please have a look at that now.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Just a second. Interpreters were not able to catch up with your speed, Mr. Bojanovic. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Enes Tabakovic was killed. That was this case. He was not detained. This was a person who was killed in a dormitory where there were other soldiers, so this was not a person who was in custody. This person was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at 1475 briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we have this Article, shall we take a look at Article 197 again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one, 197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. 244 -- 24664. Section 3 of that Article referred to the release when there has been no indictment before the expiration of period, but section 2 deals with the extension by the Supreme Court of the republic by three months, which was referred to by Ms. Sutherland. What's the relation between the two? If there was no indictment between the first initial one or three months of custody, then the investigating judge had the option to go to the Supreme Court to get another three-month extension before releasing the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The judge could, but did not necessarily have to address them. The assumption is that he could have. That's what the legislator says too, but it's up to the judge and his own assessment whether there are reasons to ask for an extension of another 90 days. In this case, I assume that the judge thought that it was unnecessary to ask for a further extension of 90 days, which would be in accordance with the law, in accordance with paragraph 3 of this Article. Since 30 days and then another 60 days had expired, there was no indictment, and quite simply he reached a decision to end custody. Let me just draw your attention to another important detail. In my practice there has been -- there hasn't been a single case of us addressing the Supreme Military Court for asking for an extension, because while the proceedings are on, then there is an automatic renewal of the custody decision. As soon as the indictment is issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did -- did we not see a decision where you asked for extension of custody? What did you talk about 1D7831? Can you upload that Exhibit MFI D3080.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is an extension of custody of 30 days that was about to be over. It's Trivkovic et al. That's the case. I continued the investigation, since not the entire investigation had been completed, not all the witnesses had been interviewed, and then I turned to the first instance Military Court, the chamber that was dealing with the case, I asked them for a 60-day extension. And you see on the next page, I think, the ruling of the criminal chamber of that court that ruled on this further extension of 60 days. So that is the first instance court. I hope that you understood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. If you just trusted me a bit more, you would see that I would come to the point. D1475, could we briefly take a look at that. The moment when --

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: The 30th of December, as you said. We don't have to look at -- for it any further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we please take a look at D1476, the 5th of January.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then the same day he issued an indictment against that person, but that is an answer that Drinic, the prosecutor acting in that case, should provide to you, really. All of us were very surprised. I don't know why the military prosecutor did that, that the same day he discontinued the investigation, dropped criminal charges, and on the very same day he brought the indictment that we see before us now. However, that's a question that you would have to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does this indictment imply and did you act in accordance with it?

utterances.text: Yes. utterances.text: Your question was not recorded.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojanovic. Thank you. I respect your work which was to our honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the summary of Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic's statement in the English language. [In English] Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic was born on 15th of May, 1938, in the village of Raca, Bijeljina municipality, where he still currently resides. He was a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS, and in 1992, he was appointed director of the Bijeljina hospital. After the SDA Muslim party was founded in Bijeljina, a reaction of the Serbs from the region was to form the Party of Democratic Accord since there was not any Serb party yet. In July 1990, Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic joined the SDS newly constituted in response the formation of SDA and HDZ. As a matter of fact, all of the members of formed Party of Democratic Accord joined the SDS collectively. In November that year, the SDS clearly won elections -- local elections in Bijeljina, but the government was constituted together with the SDA in order to improve inter-ethnic relations in the municipality. By the second half of 1990, divisions between Serbs and Muslims were clearly visible in the Bijeljina municipality. Muslims, politically initiated by the SDA leadership, openly approved of acts of terrorism by paramilitary units against the JNA in Croatia. While Serbs responded to call-up orders of the JNA commands and units, SDA leadership disseminated propaganda calling on Muslim people to ignore the call-ups. Meanwhile, the SDA planned and implemented the illegal arming of Muslims through party organs. Protests like that held at the Elvako factory instigated to ensure the appointment of the only Muslim -- Muslims were a basis for implementing the separatist policy of the SDA in Bijeljina. During this period, Dr. Kicanovic felt it was his duty to attempt to ease these tensions among the population. Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic attended meetings with the local public police station and the JNA garrison in Bijeljina regarding the security situation. He heard reports that the safety of the Serbs in the municipality was severely jeopardised by the activities of a large number of Muslims who harassed and mistreated Serbs in public places. Muslim authorities continued to illegally import weapons and distribute them to Muslim citizens. On 31st of March, 1992, Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic was openly fired at in the street. He escaped, contacted his neighbours who evacuated their families the next day. The main street -- streets were blocked by groups of the well-armed Muslims who were also randomly firing at people on the streets. Milivoje Kicanovic stayed in the village of Dvorovi to establish a dispensary to help those wounded in the fighting. Street fighting had broken out in Bijeljina, and the hospital in the town was under the control of Muslim extremists. On 3rd of April, the blockade was lifted and Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic visited the hospital, which was in a state of chaos, and Serbian patients had been severely mistreated. The media in Sarajevo reported that a massacre was committed against the Muslims, with casualties in -- in thousands. This was absolutely false. During this period, Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic and his colleagues provided medical assistance to everybody regardless of their ethnicity or religion. This included Muslims who were wounded while fighting Serbs or the JNA. Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic had direct contact with President Karadzic on several occasions. President Karadzic urged everyone to do their utmost to defuse the tensions between Serbs and Muslims in Bijeljina and to do everything possible for the welfare of all citizens. He genuinely wished to prevent what was in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When President Karadzic visited the hospital in Bijeljina, he insisted on seeing all the patients and remarked publicly that patients' ethnicity was irrelevant to him as they were foremost human beings. From Dr. Milivoje Kicanovic's family house, he could see columns of Serbian refugees travelling to take refuge in Serbia. Following the fall of Serbian Krajina in the Republic of Croatia, columns of refugees passed by continuously for four full days and nights. The local authorities provided assistance in food and medicine for those people. And that would be the summary. At that moment I do not have questions for Dr. Kicanovic.
